name: Security of Connected Medical Devices
title: Security of Connected Medical Devices
answer: Security of connected medical devices covers the protection of devices that exchange data over networks, including infusion pumps, patient monitors, imaging systems, wearables, and implantables, along with their mobile apps, cloud services, and update channels. It sits inside the broader governance field of medical device security, where the goals are not only confidentiality and privacy but also integrity, availability, and patient safety. A compromised device can affect care directly, so security work here is tied to clinical risk management and regulatory review. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, and connected devices are one setting where such models are governed. This scope includes the full lifecycle, from design and manufacture through deployment, maintenance, and retirement.

It sits inside the broader governance field of medical device security, where the goals are not only confidentiality and privacy but also integrity, availability, and patient safety. A compromised device can affect care directly, so security work here is tied to clinical risk management and regulatory review. The site tracks 1000 medical AI models, and connected devices are one setting where such models are governed. This scope includes the full lifecycle, from design and manufacture through deployment, maintenance, and retirement.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Connected medical devices run on constrained hardware, often microcontrollers or embedded Linux systems with limited memory, processing power, and battery life. They connect through Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular, or proprietary wireless links to hospital networks, gateways, and cloud services. Many rely on mobile apps, identity systems, update servers, and third-party components, which expands the attack surface beyond the device itself. Long service lives mean some devices remain in use for years after their software support ends, so patching and compatibility are persistent concerns. Security controls must fit these constraints, which is why segmentation, authenticated updates, and monitoring at the network edge are common.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through a secure development lifecycle that starts with threat modeling and risk assessment, then continues with secure coding, code review, and penetration testing before release. Teams maintain a software bill of materials to track third-party and open source components, and they use coordinated vulnerability disclosure to receive and handle reports from researchers. After deployment, the work shifts to patch management, network segmentation, runtime monitoring, and incident response, with logs and alerts feeding into clinical and security operations. Regulatory submissions often require evidence of these practices, and postmarket surveillance keeps the device under review as threats change. Documentation, traceability, and repeatable processes matter as much as any single tool.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk here cover patient privacy, data ownership, intellectual property, and the legal exposure that follows a breach or a safety failure. Provenance matters because a device is assembled from firmware, libraries, models, and services from many suppliers, and each link in that chain needs verifiable origin, integrity, and update authenticity. The site's 219 compliance and regulation pages reflect how much of this field is about evidence, audits, and standards such as IEC 62304, ISO 14971, and ISO 27001. The site also tracks 6 active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies, which shows that failures in connected care can become legal matters rather than only technical ones. Governance work therefore joins security, clinical risk, privacy, and legal review into one record that can be inspected by regulators and courts.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more connectivity, more remote monitoring, and more AI at the edge, which will keep expanding the number of devices that need identity, updates, and monitoring. Zero trust principles, hardware root of trust, and secure enclaves are moving from niche to expected in new designs, while postmarket surveillance and threat intelligence sharing are becoming continuous rather than periodic. As the site's catalogue of 1000 medical AI models grows, the line between device security and model security is likely to blur, because a model update can change clinical behavior as much as a firmware update. Regulators are converging on requirements for premarket cybersecurity and postmarket management, and manufacturers are being pushed to plan for support long after launch. The open question is how to keep older devices safe when they cannot be patched, which will keep governance and procurement under pressure.
